properties.notes: The Fossatum Africae was a fortified ditch-and-wall system that ran for hundreds of kilometers along Rome's southern North African frontier, channeling nomadic herders through controlled gates and separating farmland from the pre-desert steppe. This central Numidian stretch, mapped in detail from the air by French archaeologist Jean Baradez in the 1940s, runs through the El Kantara gorge that Trajan's Third Augustan Legion nicknamed the Kick of Hercules and down toward Biskra. Building began under Trajan and continued under Hadrian, with earthen banks three to six meters wide and forts and watchtowers at intervals along its length.

By 117 CE the Limes Germanicus ran as a cleared forest road studded with wooden watchtowers roughly every seven hundred meters, linking the Rhine at Rheinbrohl across the Taunus hills, down to the Main near Miltenberg, and on in a near-ruler-straight line to Lorch before joining the Danube frontier further east. Domitian cut the first clearings here in the 80s CE and Trajan filled out the tower chain and forts through his reign; the continuous timber palisade that later connected the towers was a Hadrianic addition of 119-120 CE, and so did not yet exist at this snapshot.

The Limes Alutanus was Trajan's new eastern frontier for Dacia, a line of forts and an earthwork vallum running up the Olt river valley to seal the province's border against the Roxolani and other groups beyond. Building began immediately after the province's conquest in 106 CE; this stretch links the fort chain from the mountain gateway at Pons Vetus down through Castra Traiana, Buridava, Pons Aluti, and Rusidava as the valley opens onto the Wallachian plain. Hadrian later thickened the same line with additional forts at Arutela and Praetorium.

properties.name_english: Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus Aqueduct
properties.notes: The Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus ran side by side from springs near Subiaco to Rome, entering the city on a shared double-tier arcade at Porta Maggiore. Claudius dedicated the line in 52 CE after Caligula began it, carrying water some 69 kilometers to the Esquiline tanks. Both channels stayed in full service in 117 CE, still visible today where their arches cross the Parco degli Acquedotti. This route traces springs, Tivoli, and the surviving arcade, not a fully surveyed channel.

The Aqua Marcia ran roughly 91 kilometers from springs near Arsoli in the upper Anio valley, staying underground for 80 kilometers before rising onto arches into Rome. The praetor Quintus Marcius Rex built it between 144 and 140 BCE, and it was prized above every other aqueduct for the coldness of its water. By 117 CE it had carried that spring water into the city for over two and a half centuries, entering near the Porta Tiburtina on its stacked arcade.

Trajan inaugurated this aqueduct on 24 June 109 CE, tapping springs on Lake Bracciano's northwest shore and running some 57 kilometers southeast into Rome. It crossed the Tiber and climbed the Janiculum, becoming the only aqueduct serving Trastevere, and it fed Trajan's new baths on the Oppian Hill. At this map's snapshot the line was barely eight years old. It later powered the Janiculum's flour mills, which briefly decided Rome's fate during the Gothic siege of 537.

This aqueduct carried water from springs at Uzes to the colony of Nemausus, winding about 50 kilometers to cover a straight-line distance of only 20 while dropping just 17 meters. Built in the first century CE, its most famous stretch is the Pont du Gard, a three-tiered bridge nearly 49 meters high that still carries visitors across the Gardon. Water reaching the city was split at the castellum divisorium, a round stone tank. The system was fully operational in 117 CE.

The Segovia aqueduct carried water some 17 kilometers from the Fuenfria spring into the city, finishing with granite arches through the Plaza del Azoguejo that stack two tiers and reach nearly 29 meters. It was built without mortar, its blocks held by precise cutting and gravity alone. A fragmentary inscription names Trajan ordering restoration, and a Trajanic coin turned up in its arches, so it was very likely already running by 117 CE despite the debated exact date.

This 132-kilometer aqueduct carried water from Djebel Zaghouan north to Carthage, ending in the La Malga cisterns, which could hold roughly 50,000 cubic meters. Hadrian ordered its construction after a drought, with work starting around 128 CE and its water temple dedicated in 139 CE. That places the system after this map's snapshot: on 11 August 117 CE, Trajan had just died and the project still lay a decade off, so Carthage still relied on older wells and cisterns.

Augustus built this aqueduct between 33 and 12 BCE to supply his fleet at Misenum, running roughly 100 kilometers from springs at Serino down to the Gulf of Naples. It branched to serve at least ten towns, including Pompeii and Herculaneum, before ending at the vast Piscina Mirabilis reservoir. It was the only Roman aqueduct built at this scale for both military and civilian use, and by 117 CE had delivered water for a century and a half. This route traces springs, towns, and terminus only.

This aqueduct carried water 6 kilometers from the Proserpina reservoir into Emerita Augusta, arriving on arches later nicknamed the Aqueduct of the Miracles, since locals assumed only divine help explained such tall piers. Thirty-eight pillars still stand up to 25 meters high, in alternating bands of brick and stone. It formed one of three aqueduct systems feeding the colony founded for Augustus's veterans in 25 BCE, and was fully functioning in 117 CE.

Herod the Great built this aqueduct to supply his new harbor city of Caesarea, channeling springs near Shuni by Mount Carmel some 23 kilometers down the coast on a raised stone channel. Construction began around 22 BCE, alternating buried sections with arched crossings. In 117 CE only this single Herodian channel ran; the parallel channel that doubled its capacity was a Hadrianic addition built after Trajan's death. Its arches still frame the beach north of the ancient city today.

Censor Manius Curius Dentatus funded this aqueduct in 272 BCE with plunder seized from defeating Pyrrhus of Epirus, making it Rome's second aqueduct and by far its longest yet built. It ran some 64 kilometers from a spring near Vicovaro down the Aniene valley and around toward the Alban Hills, staying almost entirely underground to protect the water from tampering and enemy attack. Sextus Julius Frontinus, the empire's water commissioner, still measured its flow in his official survey of Rome's aqueducts only a few decades before Trajan's death. Travelers along the Via Latina could see almost none of it, since staying hidden was the entire point of how it was built.

Censors built the Aqua Tepula in 126 BCE to tap warm springs in the Alban Hills southeast of Rome, giving the city its fourth aqueduct and, true to its name, distinctly lukewarm water. Marcus Agrippa overhauled the system in 33 BCE, laying a new 23-kilometer line called the Aqua Julia into the very same channel and stacking both aqueducts above the older Aqua Marcia so that three separate water supplies ran on one shared arcade into the city. Riders entering Rome along the Via Latina in 117 CE passed beneath this triple-decked wall of arches, each tier carrying a different aqueduct built more than a century apart from the others. All three still delivered water to fountains and bathhouses near the Porta Maggiore under Trajan.

Engineers at Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium finished this aqueduct around 80 CE, tapping a spring near Nettersheim in the Eifel hills and running the water some 95 kilometers downhill by gravity alone to the Rhine frontier capital. The flowing water deposited a hard mineral crust inside the channel as it traveled, and modern quarries around Cologne still cut this fossilized calcium carbonate as polished 'Eifel marble' tabletops today. The entire route stayed buried underground rather than crossing valleys on arches, an engineering choice that helped keep it running for roughly 180 years. Hikers can still follow marked stretches of the ancient channel through the same Eifel forest Roman surveyors once walked.

Julius Caesar personally funded this aqueduct for Antioch on the Orontes after visiting the city in 47 BCE, making it the first Roman-built aqueduct anywhere outside Italy. It carried water roughly 11 kilometers down from springs at Daphne, the wooded sanctuary suburb where Apollo was said to have chased the nymph he loved, alternating between covered channels, tunnels, and stretches carried on two-story arcades depending on the terrain. A major earthquake struck the city in 37 CE and damaged the line, but Antioch rebuilt rather than abandon it. By 117 CE the city's abundant, well-managed water supply had helped make it one of the healthiest and most celebrated metropolises of the Roman East.

Forum Julii's engineers built this aqueduct in the 1st century CE, tapping the Foux spring near Montauroux and the Siagnole spring near Mons and running the combined flow nearly 40 kilometers down to the naval harbor town below. The channel supplied roughly 2,900 cubic meters of water a day, moving through vaulted underground galleries three meters wide before crossing the final stretch on arcades still visible marching toward the old Roman gate. Augustus had built Forum Julii as his purpose-made naval base for the western Mediterranean fleet, and this aqueduct kept its shipyards, baths, and growing population running for roughly four centuries. Long sections of the arcade still stand in the countryside north of modern Fréjus.

Augustus founded Nikopolis in 31 BCE to commemorate his victory at Actium, and Roman engineers built this 50-kilometer aqueduct to give the new city a water supply worthy of its name, tapping the headwaters of the Louros river near the village now called Agios Georgios. The line dropped only about 80 meters in elevation across its entire length, an extraordinarily gentle gradient that surveyors held constant through tunnels, covered channels, and arcaded crossings over the hillier ground near Philippias. It fed twin cisterns at Nikopolis's monumental nymphaeum, the ornamental fountain house where the young city showed off its water supply to arrivals from the harbor. Ancient engineers likely finished the earliest phase under Augustus, and later Roman renovation kept the line running for centuries afterward.

Gaius Sextilius Pollio, a wealthy local benefactor, personally financed and built this aqueduct for Ephesus sometime between 4 and 14 CE, one of several channels that fed the city's fountains from springs in the hills south of town. The line ran about 3.5 kilometers into the city center, terminating near the harbor district where Pollio's adopted son later built him a memorial fountain and heroon so residents would remember exactly who had paid for their water. Ephesus was the largest city in the province of Asia and the seat of its governor, and aqueducts like this one kept its baths, fountains, and enormous population supplied straight through the High Empire. Pollio's family fountain memorial still stands near the city's State Agora today.
